msg.wifi.widthWide.fix6: Use 160 MHz or less so that the access points can use channels that do not overlap.
msg.wifi.wpa3Available: SSID {ssid} on {device} uses WPA2 only although the radio supports WPA3
msg.wifi.wpa3Available.fix: Switch to WPA2/WPA3 transition mode (protected management frames optional).
msg.wifi.wps: WPS is turned on for SSID {ssid} on {device}
msg.wifi.wps.button: WPS (push button) is turned on for SSID {ssid} on {device}
msg.wifi.wps.fix: Turn WPS off; join devices with the passphrase or a QR code instead.
msg.wifi.wps.pin: WPS (PIN) is turned on for SSID {ssid} on {device}
msg.wireless.countries: Radios at site {site} use different country codes ({parts})
msg.wireless.countries.fix: Set the same country code, the one of the country the site is in, on every radio.
msg.wireless.differs.client_isolation: SSID {ssid} at site {site}: client isolation differs ({parts})
msg.wireless.differs.client_isolation.fi: Set the same client isolation for {ssid} on every access point.
msg.wireless.differs.hidden: SSID {ssid} at site {site}: hidden setting differs ({parts})
msg.wireless.differs.hidden.fix: Set the same hidden setting for {ssid} on every access point.
msg.wireless.differs.passphrase_fingerpr: Set the same passphrase for {ssid} on every access point.
msg.wireless.differs.pmf: SSID {ssid} at site {site}: protected management frames (PMF) differs ({parts})
msg.wireless.differs.pmf.fix: Set the same protected management frames (PMF) for {ssid} on every access point.
msg.wireless.differs.roaming_80211k: SSID {ssid} at site {site}: neighbour reports (802.11k) differs ({parts})
msg.wireless.differs.roaming_80211k.fix: Set the same neighbour reports (802.11k) for {ssid} on every access point.
msg.wireless.differs.roaming_80211r: SSID {ssid} at site {site}: fast roaming (802.11r) differs ({parts})
msg.wireless.differs.roaming_80211r.fix: Set the same fast roaming (802.11r) for {ssid} on every access point.
msg.wireless.differs.roaming_80211v: SSID {ssid} at site {site}: BSS transition (802.11v) differs ({parts})
msg.wireless.differs.roaming_80211v.fix: Set the same BSS transition (802.11v) for {ssid} on every access point.
msg.wireless.differs.security: SSID {ssid} at site {site}: security mode differs ({parts})
msg.wireless.differs.security.fix: Set the same security mode for {ssid} on every access point.
msg.wireless.differs.segment_id.fix: Set the same network (VLAN) for {ssid} on every access point.
msg.wireless.noCountry: {radio} has no country code set (or did not report it)
msg.wireless.noCountry.fix: Set the country code of this radio to the country it is used in.
msg.wireless.noSubnet: SSID {ssid} on {device} uses {segment}, which has no subnet on the router
msg.wireless.noSubnet.fix: Create this VLAN with an address and DHCP on the router, or bind the SSID to a network that exists there.
msg.wireless.noSubnetUnknown: No router at site {site} reported its subnets, so it is not known whether the networks of {ssids} exist there
msg.wireless.overlap.fix: Move one of the access points to a channel that does not overlap, or use a narrower width.
msg.wireless.overlap.fix24: Move one of the access points to a channel that does not overlap (1, 6 or 11).
net.noneKnownHint: Signalbox shows {what} once a device that reports them has been read.
probes.off: Probes are off: this lists only servers the devices report (their own leases, rogue DHCP alerts). With probes.enabled: true Signalbox's host also asks every network it is attached to who answers DHCP and router solicitations.
probes.on: Signalbox's host sends one DHCPDISCOVER (never a request: no lease is taken) and one IPv6 router solicitation on each network it is attached to. Servers that are no device Signalbox knows are findings.
probes.title: DHCP servers and routers answering
rule.ack.expired.explanation: An acknowledgement of a finding has passed its end date, so the finding counts as a problem again if it still exists. Renew the acknowledgement or remove it.
rule.ack.expired.title: Acknowledgement expired
rule.addr.client-subnet.explanation: A client uses an address that does not belong to the subnet of the network it is in, or addresses of two networks at once. It has a stale fixed address, got a lease from a second DHCP server, or sits in another VLAN than expected (for example through a port or access point that joins two networks). The result is often "connected but no internet", or guests reaching the main network.
rule.addr.client-subnet.title: Client address outside its network
rule.addr.double-nat.explanation: A router gets its internet (WAN) address from another router at the site, or a private or carrier-grade NAT address from the provider, so traffic is translated twice. Browsing works, but port forwards, VPN servers, many games and VoIP calls fail or need settings on both routers, IPv6 prefix delegation often stops at the first router, and it is unclear which device is the router. Reported as information: it is often intended (a firewall behind the provider's router). With the firewalls of both routers read (#135), port forwards on the inner router that the outer router does not pass on are reported separately as a warning: from the internet they cannot work.
rule.addr.double-nat.title: Router behind another router (double NAT)
rule.addr.duplicate-ip.explanation: The same IP address belongs to devices with different MAC addresses (seen as clients or set as DHCP reservations). Only one of them can work at a time.
rule.addr.duplicate-ip.title: Address used by more than one device
rule.addr.gateway-position.explanation: Most people and devices with a fixed configuration expect the router at the first address of a subnet (.1 in a /24), some at the last. A router in the middle of the range, or networks of one site that mix both conventions, are a frequent cause of manually configured devices without internet.
rule.addr.gateway-position.title: Router address at an unusual position
rule.addr.one-gateway.explanation: Two devices act as router on the same network, typically the internet provider's router and a firewall, or an access point still in router mode. Clients get a different default gateway depending on which one answered first: some bypass the firewall, and port forwards, VPN or parental controls work only for some devices.
rule.addr.one-gateway.title: More than one router on a network
rule.addr.prefix-consistent.explanation: A switch, access point or other device on a network has an address outside the router's subnet, or the right address with another mask. It cannot reach its gateway (or reaches only part of the network): it becomes unreachable from other networks, loses time and updates, and often keeps an old factory address.
rule.addr.prefix-consistent.title: Device address does not match the router's subnet
rule.addr.subnet-overlap.explanation: Two different networks (VLANs, or networks at different sites) use overlapping address ranges. Routers cannot tell where to send traffic for those addresses, so some devices become unreachable.
rule.addr.subnet-overlap.title: Subnets overlap
rule.annotations.stale.explanation: A note or an acknowledgement names an object by its id. When a port is renamed, a VLAN moves or a device is removed, the id no longer exists and the note silently stops applying. Clients count as gone when not seen for the whole history period.
rule.annotations.stale.title: Annotation for an object that is gone
rule.cert.ca-expiring.explanation: A local certificate authority that expires breaks every certificate it issued: VPN clients, RADIUS servers and web interfaces signed by it are refused at once. Reported for authorities stored on a device, with the number of certificates on the same device that it issued: a warning 30 days before the expiry date, an error 7 days before and after it (the thresholds of the HTTPS certificate check). Devices that do not list their certificates are left out.
rule.cert.ca-expiring.title: Certificate authority on a device is expired or about to expire
rule.cert.renewed.explanation: A device that regenerates its certificate (after a firmware update, a reset or when the old one expired) no longer matches the fingerprint Signalbox pinned, so it is not read until the new one is trusted. This explains that status, with the expiry dates of the old and the new certificate, so a renewal is not mistaken for an attack. Compare the fingerprint with the device before trusting it.
rule.cert.renewed.title: Device presented a new HTTPS certificate
rule.cert.vpn-expiring.explanation: A VPN server or peer whose certificate expires stops accepting connections, often without any sign on the device until the first user is turned away. Reported for stored certificates a device names in its VPN configuration (MikroTik IPsec, OpenVPN and SSTP): a warning 30 days before the expiry date, an error 7 days before and after it (the thresholds of the HTTPS certificate check, under `certificates` in the configuration). Authorities are reported by `cert.ca-expiring`. Devices that do not list their certificates, and certificates whose use the device does not say, are left out.
rule.cert.vpn-expiring.title: Certificate used by a VPN is expired or about to expire
rule.cert.weak-key.explanation: A certificate with an RSA key shorter than 2048 bits or a SHA-1 (or MD5) signature can be forged with today's means, and current browsers refuse it. Reported for the certificate the device presents once it is trusted. Elliptic-curve and Ed25519 keys are not checked.
rule.cert.weak-key.title: HTTPS certificate with a weak key or signature
rule.clients.category-network.explanatio: The point of an IoT network is that cheap, rarely updated devices cannot reach the computers and the NAS. One camera left on the main network defeats it, and nobody notices because it works. The kind of each device comes from its annotation (category); a device with an expected network is checked by clients.unexpected-network instead. Needs an IoT network whose purpose is declared or reported, not guessed.
rule.clients.category-network.title: IoT device on the main network, or a computer in the IoT network
rule.clients.duplicate-hostname.explanat: Local DNS (Unbound, dnsmasq, the router) registers devices by the name they announce. When two devices on one network call themselves the same, only one of them is reachable by that name and the name flips between them: remote access, printing or backups go to the wrong machine. Often a cloned SD card or virtual machine, or two devices with their factory name. Generic names such as 'android' or 'iphone' are ignored.
rule.clients.duplicate-hostname.title: Two devices use the same host name
rule.clients.network-changed.explanation: A device that suddenly appears in the guest or main network usually joined the wrong SSID or was plugged into another port; a server that moves between VLANs breaks firewall rules. A mis-tagged port often shows up like this first. Reported for a week after the move. Randomised MAC addresses and clients that move back and forth often are ignored.
rule.clients.network-changed.title: Client moved to another network
rule.clients.random-mac.explanation: Phones, tablets and laptops use a private (randomised) MAC address per Wi-Fi network by default (Android 10, iOS 14, Windows 11 and later) and change it from time to time. A DHCP reservation or a DNS name for such an address works until the device picks a new one; then it gets another address and port forwards, firewall rules and parental controls stop applying to it. Virtual machines and containers use such addresses too, but keep them. The share of randomised addresses per network is shown for information: it explains why client lists grow and reservations do not stick.
rule.clients.random-mac.title: DHCP reservation or DNS name for a randomised MAC address
rule.clients.unexpected-network.explanat: You said which network a device belongs in (its annotation), and it is seen in another one: it joined the wrong SSID or sits on a port with the wrong VLAN. Only clients with a known network are checked.
rule.clients.unexpected-network.title: Client is not in the network it belongs in
rule.cloud.enabled.explanation: MyFRITZ! (Fritz!Box), MikroTik Cloud (`/ip/cloud`) and Omada Cloud access (controller setting) connect the device to its vendor's servers: the vendor then knows the device and its public address, and a vendor account can be a way to manage it from the internet. Often wanted for remote access or a dynamic DNS name, often forgotten; the check only says that it is on and what it means, and does not judge it. Reported once per device and service.
rule.cloud.enabled.title: Vendor cloud management is on
rule.device.down-long.explanation: A device that does not answer for hours is not a missed poll: it is off, was replaced (new address or certificate), or its password changed. Every check involving it uses data from before the outage or is incomplete. Reported after an hour, as an error after a day; the per-round read finding stays, this one says for how long.
rule.device.down-long.title: Device unreachable for a long time
rule.device.flapping.explanation: A device that stops answering several times a day and comes back has a power problem (PoE budget, failing power supply), overheats, restarts by itself, or sits behind a flapping link. Users notice short outages but rarely connect them to one device.
rule.device.flapping.title: Device keeps dropping out
rule.device.reboot.explanation: Unplanned restarts are a symptom of power problems (PoE budget, failing power supply), overheating, memory exhaustion or firmware crashes. A restart is seen when the device's boot time (from its uptime) moves between two observations. Restarts the device reports as a firmware update or as started by a user are not counted. Info for a restart in the last 24 hours, warning for three or more.
rule.device.reboot.title: Device restarted unexpectedly
rule.device.resources.explanation: Low memory on small access points and routers causes random reboots and dropped clients; a CPU that is busy all the time makes the device slow to forward, answer DNS or roam clients; an overheating switch in a cupboard fails in summer. Memory counts what programs use (not the page cache); CPU load is reported only when it was high in two consecutive observations; temperatures are compared with the sensor's own limit, or a generic one.
rule.device.resources.title: Device memory, CPU or temperature above its limit
rule.dhcp.declined.explanation: A device refused the address the DHCP server offered because another device already uses it (DHCPDECLINE). Two devices on the network have the same address: one of them has a fixed address inside the pool, or two DHCP servers hand out overlapping ranges.
rule.dhcp.declined.title: DHCP address declined (address conflict)
rule.dhcp.dns-cross-network.explanation: The DNS server a DHCP server hands out lies in another network than the one it serves (for example IoT clients told to use a resolver on the main LAN). That works only if the firewall allows DNS between the networks, and on guest and IoT networks that exception also opens the main network. Without it, the clients have no name resolution.
rule.dhcp.dns-cross-network.title: DHCP hands out a DNS server in another network
rule.dhcp.dns-option.explanation: The DNS servers a DHCP server tells its clients should be the resolver of this network (a DNS service Signalbox knows, or the router). Clients that use another resolver bypass local names, filtering and ad blocking, or fail if that address does not exist.
rule.dhcp.dns-option.title: DHCP hands out an unknown DNS server
rule.dhcp.domain.explanation: Clients register and look up names with the domain their DHCP server gives them. With different domains per network, a name resolves on one VLAN and not on another; .local belongs to mDNS and breaks AirPrint and similar services. RFC 8375 recommends home.arpa for home networks.
rule.dhcp.domain.title: DHCP domain names differ or are problematic
rule.dhcp.duplicate-reservation.explanat: One MAC address has several reservations with different addresses on the same network (on one server or on two), or one host name is reserved for two devices. Which address the device gets depends on the server and the order of entries, and DNS names and port forwards point at the other one. Common after moving DHCP from one router to another.
rule.dhcp.duplicate-reservation.title: Device reserved twice on one network
rule.dhcp.foreign-server.explanation: A DHCP server that Signalbox does not know answered on this network: neither its address nor its MAC address belongs to a device Signalbox reads, and no known relay forwards to it. Clients that take its offer get its gateway and DNS servers: some lose the internet, others bypass the firewall or the filtering DNS. Seen by Signalbox's own probe (when probes are on), a device's rogue-server alert, or a device that got its own address from it.
rule.dhcp.foreign-server.title: Unknown DHCP server answers on a network
rule.dhcp.in-subnet.explanation: A DHCP pool or reservation hands out addresses that the clients of the network cannot use: outside the network's subnet (often after the subnet was resized), or the network, broadcast or router address. A reservation on the router address knocks out the gateway.
rule.dhcp.in-subnet.title: DHCP pool or reservation outside the subnet
rule.dhcp.lease-time.explanation: Very short leases cause constant DHCP traffic and short outages when the server is busy. Very long leases exhaust small pools (every visitor keeps an address) and keep moved devices on old addresses for days.
rule.dhcp.lease-time.title: DHCP lease time very short or very long
rule.dhcp.one-server.explanation: Every network (VLAN) with a router needs exactly one DHCP server that hands out addresses. With none, devices that join the network get no address; with two, they answer each other's clients with different addresses, gateways or DNS servers and connections break at random.
rule.dhcp.one-server.title: One DHCP server per network
rule.dhcp.option-121-without-router.expl: Clients that receive classless static routes (DHCP option 121) ignore the router option (RFC 3442). If the routes do not contain a default route (0.0.0.0/0), those clients lose their path to the internet.
rule.dhcp.option-121-without-router.titl: Classless static routes without a default route
rule.dhcp.pool-fixed-address.explanation: An address that a router, switch or access point uses on this network lies inside the range the DHCP server hands out. Sooner or later a client gets the same address and both stop working.
rule.dhcp.pool-fixed-address.title: Router or device address inside a DHCP pool
rule.dhcp.pool-usage.explanation: When the address pool of a network is full, new phones, guests or a replaced device get no address and fall back to 169.254.x.x. Small pools with long lease times run out quickly, because every visitor keeps an address for days.
rule.dhcp.pool-usage.title: DHCP pool (nearly) full
rule.dhcp.pools-overlap.explanation: Two address pools of the same DHCP server cover the same addresses. The server may hand out one address twice or refuse to start.
rule.dhcp.pools-overlap.title: DHCP pools overlap
rule.dhcp.relay-target-missing.explanati: A DHCP relay passes requests of its network on to a DHCP server. If that address is not a device that runs an enabled DHCP server, or no address is set, the devices of the network get no address.
rule.dhcp.relay-target-missing.title: DHCP relay forwards to no DHCP server
rule.dhcp.reservation-hostname.explanati: The host name of a DHCP reservation is not the name the device with that MAC address reports. Usually the reservation was made for another device (a replaced device or network card) or the device was renamed; DNS names derived from the reservation then point at the wrong machine.
rule.dhcp.reservation-hostname.title: Reservation name differs from the device's name
rule.dhcp.reservation-in-pool.explanatio: A static reservation uses an address from the dynamic pool. Many DHCP servers can hand that address to another client while the reserved device is offline; keeping reservations outside the pool avoids the conflict.
rule.dhcp.reservation-in-pool.title: Reserved address inside a DHCP pool
rule.dhcp.router-option.explanation: The router (default gateway) a DHCP server tells its clients must be the address of the router on that network. Otherwise clients can reach their neighbours but not the internet.
rule.dhcp.router-option.title: DHCP hands out the wrong router
rule.dhcp.self-assigned.explanation: A device that has only a 169.254.x.x address gave up waiting for a DHCP answer: the DHCP server is down, its pool is full, the VLAN does not reach the server, or a firewall blocks DHCP. The user only sees "no internet" on that device.
rule.dhcp.self-assigned.title: Clients with a self-assigned address
rule.dhcp.stale-reservation.explanation: A reservation whose device has not been seen for weeks blocks an address, keeps DNS names and port forwards pointing to it, and the address may later be handed to another device. Checked once Signalbox has observed the network for the whole history period (history.days, default 30 days), and only at sites where a device reports clients.
rule.dhcp.stale-reservation.title: DHCP reservation for a device that is gone
rule.dhcp.static-in-pool.explanation: A device uses an address from the range a DHCP server hands out, but the server did not give it to the device. Sooner or later the server leases the same address to another device and both lose their connection at random. Typical for printers, NAS and IoT devices that were configured by hand once.
rule.dhcp.static-in-pool.title: Fixed address inside the DHCP pool
rule.dns.conflicting-records.explanation: The same name has different addresses on different DNS resolvers of a site. Clients get different answers depending on which resolver they ask: it works on the phone but not on the laptop. IPv4 and IPv6 records of a name are compared separately; identical round-robin sets are fine.
rule.dns.conflicting-records.title: DNS name resolves differently on two resolvers
rule.dns.forwarder-loop.explanation: DNS resolvers forward to each other in a circle (or one forwards to itself). Every lookup that is not cached goes round until it times out, often only after a reboot cleared the caches. Typical when a local filter (Pi-hole, AdGuard) forwards to the router and the router was set to forward to the filter. Two DNS servers on one device (AdGuard Home on port 53, Unbound on another port) are not a loop.
rule.dns.forwarder-loop.title: DNS forwarders form a loop
rule.dns.forwarder-missing.explanation: A resolver forwards to, or a DHCP server hands out, a DNS server with an address on a local network that no known device, DNS service or client uses. A Pi-hole or old server that was removed or moved leaves name resolution failing or slow while the router looks healthy.
rule.dns.forwarder-missing.title: DNS server on the local network does not exist
rule.dns.host-record-dynamic.explanation: A DNS host record points to an address from a DHCP pool that is not reserved for a device. The record is right today and wrong after the next lease change, reboot or power cut.
rule.dns.host-record-dynamic.title: DNS record points to a dynamic DHCP address
rule.dns.host-record-reservation.explana: A DNS host record has the same name as a DHCP reservation but points to a different address. When a reservation is changed and the DNS record is not, the name points to the old address: backups, media players and bookmarks fail while the device itself works. The resolver and the DHCP server are often different devices.
rule.dns.host-record-reservation.title: DNS record and DHCP reservation disagree
rule.dns.host-record-stale.explanation: A DNS host record points to an address that no known device, client or reservation uses. The name then resolves to nothing (time-outs instead of a clear error) or, worse, to whatever device gets that address next. Such records pile up after a server moved or a network was renumbered. The device may also just be off.
rule.dns.host-record-stale.title: DNS record points to an address nothing uses
rule.dns.single-forwarder.explanation: A DNS resolver forwards all lookups to a single upstream (one address, or several addresses of the same device). If that upstream is down (an ISP resolver outage, a Pi-hole update), the whole network has no name resolution although the internet connection works. A resolver without forwarders resolves itself and is not reported.
rule.dns.single-forwarder.title: DNS resolver has only one upstream
rule.firewall.duplicate-port-forward.exp: Two enabled port forwards of one router listen on the same external port, protocol and uplink. Only one of them gets the connections (which one depends on the order); the other is dead. Forwards limited to different source networks are not compared.
rule.firewall.duplicate-port-forward.tit: The same external port is forwarded twice
rule.firewall.forward-into-guest.explana: A port forward leads to an address in a guest network. Guest networks are meant for visitors' devices that nobody depends on: a service there is exposed to the internet and to every guest, and it stops working when the guest network is reset or isolated.
rule.firewall.forward-into-guest.title: Port forward into a guest network
rule.firewall.segment-without-zone.expla: A router has an address in a network, but none of its firewall zones contains that network. Its traffic then follows no zone policy: depending on the vendor it is blocked, or it bypasses the rules you wrote for the other networks. Typical after adding a VLAN. Only checked when the firewall was read completely.
rule.firewall.segment-without-zone.title: Routed network that no firewall zone covers
rule.firewall.untrusted-reaches-lan.expl: The firewall of the router between them accepts new connections from a guest, IoT or camera network to any address and port of a main or management network. A compromised smart plug or a guest's laptop can then scan and attack your computers and network devices. Reported only when the rules and policies surely allow it: a firewall that was not read or does not decide exactly, and rules that allow only some ports, stay quiet.
rule.firewall.untrusted-reaches-lan.titl: Guest or IoT network can reach the main or management network
rule.firmware.drift.explanation: Devices of the same model behave the same only on the same firmware. Different versions make problems hard to reproduce and often mean one device missed an update.
rule.firmware.drift.title: Identical devices run different firmware
rule.firmware.end-of-life.explanation: The vendor no longer publishes updates for this firmware, so security problems stay open.
rule.firmware.end-of-life.title: Firmware no longer supported
rule.firmware.update-available.explanati: The device reports a newer firmware than the one it runs. Updates often fix security problems; read the release notes and update in a maintenance window.
rule.firmware.update-available.title: Firmware update available
rule.health.fan-failed.explanation: A device with a failed fan overheats and restarts or slows down, usually on the first hot day. Reported where the device itself says the fan is not working; a fan standing still without such a verdict may be off on purpose (quiet mode).
rule.health.fan-failed.title: Fan failed
rule.health.psu-failed.explanation: A device with redundant power supplies keeps running when one fails, so nobody notices until the second one fails too. Reported where the device says a power supply is not ok (no input power or broken).
rule.health.psu-failed.title: Power supply failed
rule.health.storage-full.explanation: A full system storage (OpenWrt overlay, flash, root file system) means settings can no longer be saved and firmware or package updates fail; a full data disk stops logging. RAM-backed storage (tmpfs) is not counted: it is memory.
rule.health.storage-full.title: Device storage nearly full
rule.health.ups-not-tested.explanation: A UPS battery ages without anyone noticing; a self-test finds a dead battery before the next power cut does. Reported when the last self-test the UPS reports is more than 180 days ago; silent when it reports none.
rule.health.ups-not-tested.title: UPS not tested for a long time
rule.health.ups-on-battery.explanation: A UPS on battery means the mains power is gone (or its input is not connected): the network stops when the battery is empty.
rule.health.ups-on-battery.title: UPS running on battery
rule.health.ups-runtime-low.explanation: A UPS whose battery lasts only a few minutes at the present load cannot carry the network through a short power cut or give servers time for a clean shutdown. Usually the battery is old, or the UPS carries more load than it was meant for.
rule.health.ups-runtime-low.title: UPS runtime too short
rule.health.uptime-very-long.explanation: A device that has not restarted for more than a year has not had a firmware update in that time either (updates restart it), and some problems only show at the next restart, for example settings that were never saved.
rule.health.uptime-very-long.title: Device not restarted for over a year
rule.inventory.duplicate-device.explanat: Two devices in Signalbox have the same management address or the same port MAC address, for example a switch added directly and also reported by its controller. Every check then sees it twice: duplicate SSIDs, VLAN differences with itself, doubled clients.
rule.inventory.duplicate-device.title: Device is in the inventory twice
rule.inventory.management-address.explan: The address a device is managed at (by Signalbox, by you, by a controller) lies in a DHCP pool without a reservation. After a power cut or a long downtime it can get another address: the device seems to disappear. Two devices with the same management address cannot both be reached.
rule.inventory.management-address.title: Management address is a dynamic DHCP address
rule.inventory.unknown-neighbour.explana: A device announces itself by LLDP (or a similar protocol) with a management address, but it is not one of the devices Signalbox reads. If it is a switch or access point, VLAN paths through it stay incomplete and its SSIDs and firmware are not checked.
rule.inventory.unknown-neighbour.title: Network device seen by LLDP is not in Signalbox
rule.inventory.unknown-network-device.ex: A neighbour announces itself by LLDP, MNDP or CDP as a bridge (switch), router or WLAN access point, or describes itself as network equipment, but it is not one of the devices Signalbox reads: its chassis MAC and management address match no device or port. Without it VLAN paths through it stay incomplete and its SSIDs and firmware are not checked. Phones and stations are not reported.
rule.inventory.unknown-network-device.ti: Switch, router or access point seen by LLDP is not in Signalbox
rule.ipv6.partial.explanation: The router has IPv6 on some networks with clients but not on others, or one network has only a local (ULA) prefix while the others have global ones. Usually a network added later was forgotten when IPv6 was set up: devices there behave differently (no IPv6 reachability, other DNS paths). Turn the rule off if IPv6 is disabled there on purpose.
rule.ipv6.partial.title: IPv6 only on some client networks
rule.ipv6.prefix-64.explanation: Automatic IPv6 addressing (SLAAC) only works with a /64 prefix. With a /56, /60 or /80 on a network, clients get no IPv6 address (Android never uses DHCPv6) or only some of them do, which looks like random IPv6 breakage.
rule.ipv6.prefix-64.title: IPv6 client network does not use a /64
rule.ipv6.unknown-prefix.explanation: Clients on this network have IPv6 addresses from a prefix that none of the known routers of the network has. Another router on the network (an ISP box, a phone hotspot, a virtual machine host or a misconfigured access point) is sending router advertisements: clients get an extra address and default route, so traffic bypasses the firewall, or IPv6 connections fail and apps hang until they fall back to IPv4.
rule.ipv6.unknown-prefix.title: Clients use an IPv6 prefix no router announces
rule.lag.consistent.explanation: All member ports of a link aggregation (LAG, bond) must have the same speed, duplex and VLANs, and must be cabled to ports of one other device that form a LAG there too. A LAG on one end and single ports on the other end loops or drops traffic; members with different VLANs lose frames of some connections only. A LAG with only one working member has lost its redundancy and part of its bandwidth.
rule.lag.consistent.title: Link aggregation differs between members or ends
rule.link.mtu.explanation: Both ends of a cable should use the same MTU. Jumbo frames (MTU 9000) on one end and 1500 on the other drop only large packets: ping works, but file copies and backups hang.
rule.link.mtu.title: MTU differs between the ends of a link
rule.link.slow.explanation: A cable between two network devices (router, switch, access point) runs at 10 or 100 Mbit/s, or a port runs in half duplex. A slow uplink caps every client behind it, which looks like slow internet or slow Wi-Fi; half duplex causes collisions. Common causes are a damaged cable or connector that uses only two pairs, an old patch panel, or a port set to a fixed speed. A link slower than both ports support (1 Gbit/s on two 2.5 Gbit/s ports) is reported as info.
rule.link.slow.title: Slow or half-duplex link
rule.link.speed-duplex.explanation: The two ends of a cable report a different speed or duplex mode. This usually means a fixed setting on one side and auto-negotiation on the other, or a damaged cable, and causes slow or unreliable connections.
rule.link.speed-duplex.title: Link ends disagree on speed or duplex
rule.log.inconsistent.explanation: When the devices of one site send their syslog to different collectors, or some send it nowhere, the logs of an incident are spread over several places or missing. Reported per site when at least one device sends syslog to a remote target; devices whose log targets are not read are left out.
rule.log.inconsistent.title: Devices of a site log to different targets
rule.log.plain-transport.explanation: Syslog over UDP or TCP is not encrypted and not authenticated: whoever sits on the way can read the messages (they name users, addresses and failed logins) and add or drop some. Reported when a device sends it to a collector on the internet, to one in another network than its own management network, or across a guest, IoT or camera network. A collector in the device's own network, a host name, an address behind a VPN tunnel and syslog over TLS are not reported; neither are devices whose management network is not known.
rule.log.plain-transport.title: Syslog is sent in clear text beyond the device's own network
rule.log.target-unknown.explanation: A device that sends its syslog, flow records or SNMP traps to a private address outside every known network, or to an address in a known network that no device or client uses, most likely still points to an old collector: its messages are lost, and nobody notices until they are needed. Host names, public addresses outside the known networks and addresses behind a VPN tunnel are not checked; an unused address is only reported where clients are read for that network.
rule.log.target-unknown.title: Logs are sent to an address nobody uses
rule.mac.flapping.explanation: The same MAC address is learned on different ports or switches again and again. That is the sign of a loop in the cabling (spanning tree off or misconfigured), two devices with the same address, or a virtual machine or bonded NIC that switches between links. It causes short outages and packet loss for the device. Counted from the MAC address tables of each observation round, so only moves that last until a round are seen. Wireless roaming between access points, uplinks and addresses of network devices are ignored.
rule.mac.flapping.title: MAC address keeps moving between ports
rule.mac.static-stale.explanation: A static entry in a switch's MAC address table pins an address to a port. When the device is gone, the entry stays, and a new device that later gets the address (or is plugged into another port) is cut off or flooded. Reported when the address has not been seen anywhere (clients, any device) for 14 days, and only at sites where a device reports clients and Signalbox has observed for at least that long.
rule.mac.static-stale.title: Static MAC table entry for a device that is gone
rule.mac.table-full.explanation: A device's MAC address table has as many entries as Signalbox keeps per device (2048) or close to it (90 %). Entries beyond that are dropped, so the placement of clients and the links found through unmanaged switches may be incomplete or wrong. A large table also means a switch that floods when its own table is full: check for a loop or a device sending frames with random source addresses.
rule.mac.table-full.title: MAC address table is (nearly) full
rule.port.admin-down-with-neighbour.expl: The port is switched off in its configuration, but a cable link or an LLDP neighbour says a device is connected to it. Often a port that was disabled for a test and forgotten, or the cable is in the wrong port.
rule.port.admin-down-with-neighbour.titl: Disabled port with a connected device
rule.port.autoneg-mismatch.explanation: When one end of a cable has a fixed speed and the other uses auto-negotiation, the auto-negotiating end cannot learn the duplex mode and falls back to half duplex. The link works, but slowly and with collisions and errors.
rule.port.autoneg-mismatch.title: Auto-negotiation on only one end of a link
rule.port.description-mismatch.explanati: The description of the port names a device that Signalbox knows, but the cable link or LLDP shows another device on that port. Either the cable was moved or the description is out of date; both mislead whoever works on the network next.
rule.port.description-mismatch.title: Port description names another device than the connected one
rule.port.eee-on-uplink.explanation: Energy-efficient Ethernet (EEE, 802.3az) lets a port sleep between packets. On links between switches, routers and access points it saves little and is a known cause of link drops, added latency and interoperability problems, especially on cheap switches.
rule.port.eee-on-uplink.title: Energy-efficient Ethernet on a link between network devices
rule.port.flapping.explanation: A cable link that keeps going down and up (a bad cable or connector, a duplex or auto-negotiation problem, a failing port) causes short outages for everything behind it. Counted from the link state of each observation round, so only losses that last until a round are seen. Warning on links between network devices, info on other ports (a computer that sleeps and wakes also does this).
rule.port.flapping.title: Link goes down and up repeatedly
rule.ra.foreign-router.explanation: A router that Signalbox does not know sent IPv6 router advertisements on this network, as a default router or with prefixes for clients to take addresses from. Clients then use it as a gateway for IPv6 and may bypass the firewall, or take addresses from a prefix that does not reach the internet. Routers that only announce routes (lifetime 0, no address prefix: Thread border routers such as smart speakers) are not reported.
rule.ra.foreign-router.title: Unknown IPv6 router advertises on a network
rule.redundancy.single-point.explanation: One switch or one cable carries the connection of several access points or switches to the router. If it fails, all of them are offline. A spare, a better switch or a second uplink (with LAG or spanning tree) helps. Checked only for sites with at least three network devices whose links to the router are all known.
rule.redundancy.single-point.title: Single point of failure
rule.route.asymmetric.explanation: A static route sends a network to a second router, which answers through a third router instead of the first. Such an asymmetric path works only while no firewall on the way tracks connections; most do, and drop the answers.
rule.route.asymmetric.title: The way back between two routers differs from the way there
rule.route.default-missing.explanation: A router that connects a network to the internet sends everything it has no better route for to its default route. Without one, no device behind it can reach the internet, even though the internet connection itself is up.
rule.route.default-missing.title: A router has no default route
rule.route.multiple-default.explanation: With equal metrics it is not defined which default route carries a connection, so traffic may jump between internet connections and break logins and streams. Give the connection that should win the lower metric.
rule.route.multiple-default.title: A router has two default routes with the same metric
rule.route.no-return.explanation: A static route sends a network to a second router. If that router has no route to the networks behind the first one, requests arrive and the answers are lost, so the connection never works.
rule.route.no-return.title: A router sends traffic to another router that has no way back
rule.route.unreachable-gateway.explanati: A static route sends traffic to a next hop that the router must reach directly. If the next hop is in none of the router's own networks, the route cannot be used.
rule.route.unreachable-gateway.title: A static route's next hop is outside every network of the router
rule.route.vpn-return.explanation: A site-to-site tunnel needs routes in both directions. If the other end's peer entry for this site accepts none of this site's networks, requests arrive and the answers are dropped.
rule.route.vpn-return.title: The other end of a VPN tunnel has no route back
rule.security.certificate-expiry.explana: Signalbox pins the certificate of a device and ignores its dates, but browsers, apps and controllers do not: when it expires the web interface and everything that talks to the device over HTTPS stops working. A warning is reported 30 days before the expiry date, an error 7 days before and after it (both configurable under `certificates` in the configuration). Devices without HTTPS and certificates that are not trusted yet are left out.
rule.security.certificate-expiry.title: HTTPS certificate expired or about to expire
rule.security.insecure-services.explanat: Telnet, FTP, plain HTTP without redirect, SNMP v1/v2c with the default community, SSH login of root with a password and MAC telnet send passwords in clear text or are common attack targets, and several vendors turn them on by default (MikroTik: telnet, ftp, www, api, winbox; OpenWrt: HTTP and root password login). A service that is limited to a management network (the device's own address filter or listen setting) is reported as information only.
rule.security.insecure-services.title: Insecure management services are on
rule.security.management-exposure.explan: A switch or access point is managed at an address in a guest or IoT network (or has an address there). Guests, or a compromised smart plug, can then reach its login page: brute force and firmware exploits are one step away. A router has an address in every network it serves; whether its web interface is reachable from there depends on its firewall: where that is not read, the case is reported as not checked, otherwise security.service-exposure decides. Level 2: with the firewall rules read (#135), a management service of a device in another network that guest, IoT or camera networks reach through the router is reported too; where the firewall does not decide exactly, the rule stays quiet.
rule.security.management-exposure.title: Network device managed in a guest or IoT network
rule.security.plaintext-read.explanation: Signalbox reads this device without encryption (NETGEAR Plus NSDP, TP-Link Easy Smart, plain HTTP), so its password can be captured by any device in the network of its management address; for such switches that is the whole admin access. Reported when the network also holds clients or Wi-Fi networks: a warning if it is a guest, IoT or camera network. A separate management network without clients is quiet.
rule.security.plaintext-read.title: Device managed without encryption in a network with clients
rule.security.port-forward-target.explan: A port forward (destination NAT) on a router leads to an address that will not stay the right device or that should not be exposed: a dynamic DHCP address (the forward ends up on whatever device gets the address next), an address in no known network (a dead service), an address no known device uses, a client in an IoT or camera network (information), or a management service of a network device (an error). Disabled forwards are not checked; guest networks are firewall.forward-into-guest.
rule.security.port-forward-target.title: Port forward to an unsuitable target
rule.security.service-exposure.explanati: A management service (web interface, SSH, telnet, API, SNMP) is offered in a guest, IoT or camera network, so guests or a compromised smart plug can try to log in. Complements security.management-exposure, which looks at addresses: this one looks at where the device says it listens. A router serves every network it has an address in unless its firewall blocks the services there; where the firewall is not read or does not decide exactly, that case is reported as not checked.
rule.security.service-exposure.title: Management service offered in a guest or IoT network
rule.security.wan-management.explanation: A gateway that offers its web interface, SSH, API or another management service on the internet side is the main way home routers get compromised; remote access is often turned on once for a fix and forgotten. The device says it (Fritz!Box remote access) or the service listens on the uplink without an address filter and its firewall lets the internet in. Where the firewall is not read or does not decide exactly, the case is reported as not checked. Only gateways with a reported uplink are checked.
rule.security.wan-management.title: Management reachable from the internet
rule.segment.guest-no-isolation.explanat: Stations of a guest SSID can reach each other: one infected phone of a visitor can attack the others, and anyone with the guest password can see the devices of the other guests. Access points can block this (client isolation, AP isolation). Checked where the access point reports the setting (OpenWrt) and the network is not isolated by the device anyway.
rule.segment.guest-no-isolation.title: Guest Wi-Fi without client isolation
rule.segment.iot-on-5ghz-only.explanatio: An SSID of an IoT network is only broadcast on 5 or 6 GHz. Many smart plugs, sensors and cameras only have 2.4 GHz radios and will not see it.
rule.segment.iot-on-5ghz-only.title: IoT Wi-Fi only on 5 or 6 GHz
rule.segment.purpose-missing.explanation: The site has several networks (VLANs), but for some it is not known what they are for (main, guest, IoT, management, ...). The guest and IoT checks then rely on names or stay silent. Declare the purposes in the desired state; devices that know their guest network report it themselves.
rule.segment.purpose-missing.title: Network purposes not declared
rule.signalbox.read.explanation: A device did not answer, refused the login, presented an untrusted certificate, or one of its capabilities failed. Checks that need this data are incomplete until it is fixed.
rule.signalbox.read.title: Device could not be read completely
rule.time.dhcp-ntp-mismatch.explanation: DHCP option 42 tells clients where to get the time. An address in a local network that no device uses, or a known device that does not serve time on that network, leaves the clients that use it (many IoT devices, cameras, phones on some systems) with a wrong clock.
rule.time.dhcp-ntp-mismatch.title: DHCP hands out an NTP server that does not serve time
rule.time.no-local-ntp.explanation: With one device (usually the gateway) serving time for the site and every other device using it, clocks agree with each other and keep working while the internet is down. Reported per site for devices other than gateways that use only public NTP servers: when a device of the site serves time, or when a gateway reports that it does not. Server names that are not well-known public services may be local and are not counted.
rule.time.no-local-ntp.title: Devices ask the internet for the time
rule.time.not-synchronised.explanation: A device without NTP drifts by seconds a day and loses the time at every power cut; one with NTP configured but not synchronised cannot reach its servers (a wrong address, a firewall, no DNS). Warning when NTP is configured but not synchronised, info when no NTP server is configured. Silent where the device does not report its NTP client.
rule.time.not-synchronised.title: Device clock not synchronised
rule.time.ntp-unreachable.explanation: A device whose NTP server is an address in a local network that no device uses, or a known device that does not serve time (there), never synchronises its clock. Names and addresses outside the known networks are not checked.
rule.time.ntp-unreachable.title: NTP server of a device does not exist or serve time
rule.time.offset.explanation: Wrong clocks make logs useless when tracing a problem across devices and break TLS (certificates "not yet valid"), WPA3 and 802.1X, VPN handshakes and scheduled Wi-Fi or parental-control times. A device without a battery-backed clock starts in 1970 after a power cut until NTP corrects it. The device's clock is compared with Signalbox's at the moment it was read; the request's round trip is allowed for.
rule.time.offset.title: Device clock is wrong
rule.time.timezone.explanation: Devices with different time zones show the same event at different times in their logs and run scheduled Wi-Fi times, parental controls and reboots at the wrong hour. Compared by the offset from UTC at the time of reading, so equal zones with different names (an IANA name and a POSIX string) are not reported.
rule.time.timezone.title: Devices of one site use different time zones
rule.topology.hidden-device.explanation: Many devices, or devices of several networks, are seen behind one port that has no known neighbour. Usually an unmanaged switch or a travel router is connected there. Signalbox cannot see through it: VLAN checks through it may be wrong, it may strip or leak tagged VLANs, and a loop behind it is invisible.
rule.topology.hidden-device.title: Unknown switch or access point behind a port
rule.topology.manual-conflict.explanatio: A cable entered by hand connects two ports, but the devices themselves (LLDP or MAC tables) report that one of these ports is connected somewhere else. Either the cable was moved or the entry is wrong.
rule.topology.manual-conflict.title: Entered cable differs from what the devices report
rule.topology.untagged-only-link.explana: A link between two managed devices carries no tagged VLANs. That is fine for a network without VLANs; with VLANs it usually means a trunk was configured as an access port.
rule.topology.untagged-only-link.title: Link carries only the untagged network
rule.trace.extra-nat.explanation: A trace from the gateway to the internet passed more routers with private (RFC 1918) addresses before the first public one than Signalbox expects from the uplinks it knows: there is a router in front of the site that Signalbox does not know about (double NAT by an ISP box in router mode, a forgotten travel router). Some providers number their own routers privately; then this is expected.
rule.trace.extra-nat.title: More routers with private addresses on the way out than known
rule.trace.not-via-tunnel.explanation: A VPN tunnel of the device routes the network of the traced address to the other site, but the trace from the device went somewhere else first: the first router that answered is neither the tunnel's other end nor the target. The traffic may leave unencrypted over the internet (a missing route, a policy route, a tunnel that is down).
rule.trace.not-via-tunnel.title: Traffic to the other site does not take the tunnel
rule.vlan.client-port-mismatch.explanati: A device on an access port belongs to the port's VLAN. If its address is in another network, the port's VLAN setting is wrong, the device tags its own frames (a hypervisor, a misconfigured NAS) or a hidden switch with other VLAN settings sits in between. Where the switch reports a MAC address table, the VLAN it learned the device in counts as the port's network, and a port that learns other addresses too (a hidden switch) is skipped.
rule.vlan.client-port-mismatch.title: Wired client is in another network than its switch port
rule.vlan.management-separate.explanatio: The management addresses of routers, switches and access points lie in a network that also has user devices or an SSID, while the site already uses VLANs. Every compromised laptop or IoT device can then reach the login pages of the network devices. A separate management VLAN, reachable only from admin devices, is the usual next step. A network with the purpose management is that VLAN and is not reported; guest and IoT networks are security.management-exposure's finding. Off unless enabled: this is a recommendation, not a fault.
rule.vlan.management-separate.title: Devices are managed in a network with clients
rule.vlan.native-mismatch.explanation: Both ends of a cable must agree on which network travels untagged (the native VLAN). If they differ, devices on one network suddenly appear on the other one, or lose their connection.
rule.vlan.native-mismatch.title: Untagged VLAN differs between the ends of a link
rule.vlan.path-to-gateway.explanation: Every network (VLAN) that an access point offers on an SSID, or that a switch or access point puts on an access port, has to be carried on every cable between that device and the router that serves its addresses. If one switch on the way does not carry it, clients on that network get no address and no internet.
rule.vlan.path-to-gateway.title: VLAN does not reach the gateway
rule.vlan.single-untagged.explanation: A port sends at most one network untagged. With two untagged VLANs the device behind it sees both networks mixed (a VLAN leak). A PVID (the VLAN for incoming untagged frames) that is not the port's untagged VLAN puts incoming traffic into another network than the outgoing one: DHCP may work, nothing else does.
rule.vlan.single-untagged.title: Port is untagged in more than one VLAN, or its PVID is another VLAN
rule.vlan.tagged-both-ends.explanation: A VLAN that one end of a cable sends tagged must also be configured on the other end, otherwise its traffic is dropped there.
rule.vlan.tagged-both-ends.title: VLAN tagged on only one end of a link
rule.vlan.trunk-scope.explanation: The cable to an access point should carry only the networks (VLANs) the access point uses for its SSIDs, its own access ports and its management address. Every extra VLAN on the cable can be reached by anyone who unplugs the access point (in a hallway or outdoors), and its broadcasts flood the access point.
rule.vlan.trunk-scope.title: Link to an access point carries networks it does not use
rule.vlan.unused.explanation: The router has an address range for this network, but no switch port and no SSID uses it. It may be left over from an earlier setup.
rule.vlan.unused.title: VLAN is not used
rule.vpn.allowed-ips-overlap.explanation: A WireGuard peer receives the traffic for its allowed IPs. Two peers of one tunnel with the same network leave the traffic to only one of them; a peer that routes a network that also exists locally cuts the site off from its own devices or sends their traffic through the tunnel.
rule.vpn.allowed-ips-overlap.title: Allowed IPs of VPN peers overlap each other or a local network
rule.vpn.allowed-ips-unrouted.explanatio: The allowed IPs of a WireGuard peer only say what the tunnel accepts. For traffic to use the tunnel, the device needs a route for each network through the tunnel interface. If the configuration has none, the networks behind the peer cannot be reached.
rule.vpn.allowed-ips-unrouted.title: A VPN peer's networks are not routed into the tunnel
rule.vpn.ends-disagree.explanation: When both ends of a WireGuard tunnel are known, each must list the other as a peer, and the networks one end routes to the other must exist there. Otherwise the tunnel cannot work in one direction or at all.
rule.vpn.ends-disagree.title: The two ends of a VPN tunnel do not match
rule.vpn.handshake-stale.explanation: WireGuard peers that are meant to stay connected (a persistent keepalive is set) complete a handshake about every two minutes. Without a handshake for five minutes, or none since the tunnel came up, the other end is not answering: the site behind it is cut off.
rule.vpn.handshake-stale.title: A VPN peer has not been reached for a while
rule.vpn.keepalive-behind-nat.explanatio: A router behind NAT (a private or carrier-grade NAT address on its internet connection) keeps the NAT entry of a WireGuard tunnel only while packets flow. Without a persistent keepalive (usually 25 seconds) the entry expires when the tunnel is idle and the other end can no longer reach this one.
rule.vpn.keepalive-behind-nat.title: A VPN peer behind NAT has no persistent keepalive
rule.wan.cgnat.explanation: The provider does not give the router an IPv4 address of its own on the internet: it shares one address among many customers (carrier-grade NAT, 100.64.0.0/10, or DS-Lite). Outgoing connections work, but nothing on the internet can connect in over IPv4: port forwards, a VPN server at home and remote access to cameras or a NAS do not work.
rule.wan.cgnat.title: Internet connection is behind carrier-grade NAT
rule.wan.dns-mismatch.explanation: The router forwards DNS lookups to an address on the network of its internet connection (the provider's or the modem's side), but the provider now hands out other DNS servers there and no known device uses that address. Typical after a modem or provider change: the old address was typed in and now answers slowly or not at all. Forwarding to any other resolver (a public one, a Pi-hole, a filter) is a choice and not reported.
rule.wan.dns-mismatch.title: Router forwards DNS to an address the provider no longer hands out
rule.wan.down.explanation: A gateway reports that one of its internet connections is not connected (no address, no PPP session). With no other connection, the site is offline; with a backup line, the site runs on the backup.
rule.wan.down.title: Internet connection is down
rule.wan.no-ipv6.explanation: The provider delegated an IPv6 prefix to the router, but none of the site's networks with clients has a global IPv6 subnet. Devices only use IPv4, through NAT, although the line has native IPv6: no direct reachability from the internet (useful behind carrier-grade NAT) and some services are slower. ``ipv6.partial`` reports a site where only some networks have IPv6.
rule.wan.no-ipv6.title: Provider gives IPv6, but no network uses it
rule.wifi.24-channel-plan.explanation: On 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap. A radio in between (for example 3 or 8) overlaps two of them and suffers from every neighbour that uses the standard plan. wifi.channel-overlap only compares your own access points; this rule is about the neighbours. Where channel 13 is allowed (outside North America), 1, 5, 9 and 13 is also accepted. Radios on automatic channel selection are skipped.
rule.wifi.24-channel-plan.title: 2.4 GHz radio between the standard channels
rule.wifi.6ghz-h2e.explanation: On 6 GHz, WPA3 must derive the SAE password with hash-to-element (H2E); with the older hunting-and-pecking method only, 6 GHz clients cannot join. Only WPA3-only networks are checked here (other modes are not allowed on 6 GHz, see wifi.6ghz-security).
rule.wifi.6ghz-h2e.title: WPA3 on 6 GHz without hash-to-element (H2E)
rule.wifi.6ghz-security.explanation: The Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 specifications allow only WPA3 and Enhanced Open (OWE) on 6 GHz. With WPA2, WPA2/WPA3 transition mode or an open network, clients do not show or cannot join the network on that band, so nothing uses the 6 GHz radio. A common result of copying the 2.4/5 GHz settings to the new radio. Protected management frames, which 6 GHz also requires, are checked by wifi.pmf.
rule.wifi.6ghz-security.title: Wi-Fi on 6 GHz without WPA3 or OWE
rule.wifi.channel-overlap.explanation: Two access points of the same site send on channels that overlap in the same band, so they take turns instead of working in parallel and the Wi-Fi gets slower for everyone. Signalbox does not know which access points can hear each other, so every pair at one site counts as neighbours. 2.4 GHz channels overlap when they are less than 5 apart (use 1, 6 and 11); 5 and 6 GHz channels overlap when their 20/40/80/160 MHz blocks share a 20 MHz channel.
rule.wifi.channel-overlap.title: Access points on overlapping channels
rule.wifi.channel-width.explanation: On 2.4 GHz a 40 MHz channel covers two thirds of the band and collides with every neighbour; most clients fall back to 20 MHz anyway and throughput drops for everyone. On 5 GHz (160 MHz) and 6 GHz (320 MHz), very wide channels leave no room for several access points to use channels that do not overlap.
rule.wifi.channel-width.title: Channel too wide for the band or the number of access points
rule.wifi.country.explanation: The country code tells a radio which channels and transmit power are allowed where it is used. Without it, radios fall back to a restrictive world setting (fewer channels, lower power); with different codes, access points of one site disagree about which channels exist and clients may not find them after roaming.
rule.wifi.country.title: Wi-Fi country code missing or different
rule.wifi.default-ssid.explanation: An SSID such as OpenWrt, MikroTik-1A2B3C or FRITZ!Box 7590 XY means the access point was never set up: often open (OpenWrt) or with the password printed on the label, in the default network, and it tells everyone nearby which device it is. Turn the rule off if you kept a factory name on purpose.
rule.wifi.default-ssid.title: Wi-Fi network with a factory SSID
rule.wifi.dfs.explanation: On 5 GHz channels 52-144 an access point must listen for radar for a minute after it starts (ten minutes on 120-128 in Europe) and leave the channel when it detects one; its clients then lose the network. Short unexplained Wi-Fi outages, or an access point that takes minutes to come back after a reboot, are often DFS. Some clients do not support these channels at all. DFS channels are allowed and often needed: this is for information, turn the rule off if you use them on purpose.
rule.wifi.dfs.title: 5 GHz radio on a radar (DFS) channel
rule.wifi.guest-isolation.explanation: A guest SSID puts its clients into the same network (VLAN) as the main LAN or as other, non-guest SSIDs. The guest password is shared freely; guests then reach the NAS, printers and admin pages. Guest SSIDs are those declared as guest in the desired state or named like one (guest, gast, visitor; then only a warning). A guest network the device reports itself (Fritz!Box guest access, Omada guest network) is kept apart by that device and not checked.
rule.wifi.guest-isolation.title: Guest Wi-Fi shares a network with the main LAN
rule.wifi.hidden.explanation: A hidden SSID is not secret: every phone that knows it calls out its name wherever it goes, which tells strangers which networks it knows, and some devices join or roam badly. Hiding adds no security; the password does. Hidden SSIDs that serve as a wireless uplink between two access points are skipped.
rule.wifi.hidden.title: Hidden Wi-Fi network
rule.wifi.passphrase-reuse.explanation: If a guest network has the passphrase of the main network, giving it to visitors gives them the main network as well, and separate networks (VLANs) are worth nothing. Compared across different SSIDs of a site by a keyed digest that is never shown. Not reported: the same SSID on several radios or access points, and SSIDs that put clients into the same network (for example one SSID per band), because they are one network anyway.
rule.wifi.passphrase-reuse.title: Different Wi-Fi networks use the same passphrase
rule.wifi.pmf.explanation: WPA3 and Enhanced Open (OWE) require protected management frames (PMF, 802.11w): without them it is not WPA3, and many phones and laptops refuse to connect or connect unreliably. In WPA2/WPA3 transition mode, PMF turned off keeps every client on WPA2. Vendors show PMF as a separate setting, so this mismatch happens easily.
rule.wifi.pmf.title: Protected management frames do not match the security mode
rule.wifi.segment-at-gateway.explanation: The Wi-Fi network puts its clients into a VLAN for which no router has an address. Clients connect but get no IP address and cannot reach anything. A network a router keeps to itself (an isolated guest network without a subnet in the model, such as the Fritz!Box guest Wi-Fi) is served by that router and not reported.
rule.wifi.segment-at-gateway.title: Wi-Fi network bound to a network the router does not serve
rule.wifi.segment-weakest-link.explanati: A network (VLAN) is only as protected as the weakest Wi-Fi network (SSID) that puts clients into it. An open SSID in the same VLAN as the private Wi-Fi gives everyone nearby the private network; it happens when an extra SSID is created without choosing a VLAN and joins the default bridge. Two password-protected SSIDs with different passwords on one network are often deliberate, but then only the password separates them.
rule.wifi.segment-weakest-link.title: Weaker Wi-Fi network shares a network with a protected one
rule.wifi.ssid-consistent.explanation: A Wi-Fi network (SSID) that is broadcast by several access points must be set up the same way on all of them. Phones and laptops remember one set of settings per name: when they move to an access point with a different security mode, password or VLAN, they fail to connect or end up on the wrong network. Different roaming or PMF settings make roaming slow or unreliable. Passwords are only compared by a fingerprint and never shown. Where a scan heard your own access points (#169), the security each BSSID announces is compared with its settings too.
rule.wifi.ssid-consistent.title: Wi-Fi network set up differently on access points
rule.wifi.ssid-count.explanation: Every SSID sends its own beacons at the lowest data rate, about ten times a second. With many SSIDs on one radio, beacons alone take a noticeable share of the airtime (10-20 % on 2.4 GHz with five SSIDs) and every client gets slower. Hidden SSIDs beacon too. Often several SSIDs could be one, or a network nobody uses can be turned off.
rule.wifi.ssid-count.title: Radio broadcasts many SSIDs
rule.wifi.ssid-coverage.explanation: A Wi-Fi network (SSID) that only some access points of a site broadcast, or that is on 5 GHz at some and only on 2.4 GHz at others, makes roaming clients lose the network or end up on the slow band near one access point. Usually it was added to one access point and forgotten on the others. wifi.ssid-consistent only compares the access points that have the SSID. Guest networks limited to one area are common: turn the rule off if that is intended.
rule.wifi.ssid-coverage.title: Wi-Fi network missing on some access points or bands
rule.wifi.tx-power.explanation: Clients pick the strongest signal. A 2.4 GHz radio louder than the 5 GHz radio of the same SSID keeps them on the slow band; one loud access point attracts clients from far away while closer ones stay idle, and roaming suffers. Radios with automatic or unreported power are skipped.
rule.wifi.tx-power.title: Transmit power unbalanced between bands or access points
rule.wifi.weak-security.explanation: An open network lets anyone nearby join and read unencrypted traffic, WEP and TKIP are broken, and WPA version 1 and WPA/WPA2 mixed mode keep the weak TKIP cipher available. Old ciphers also force slow legacy rates on the whole radio. An open guest network is only a warning (Enhanced Open, OWE, is better); the other findings are errors, except WPA/WPA2 mixed mode and TKIP offered next to AES, which are warnings.
rule.wifi.weak-security.title: Wi-Fi network with open, WEP, WPA1 or TKIP security
rule.wifi.wpa3-available.explanation: WPA3 protects weak passphrases against offline guessing and gives forward secrecy. In WPA2/WPA3 transition mode old devices keep working, so there is rarely a reason to stay on WPA2 only when the radio supports WPA3. Quiet where the access point did not report what its radios support.
rule.wifi.wpa3-available.title: WPA2-only Wi-Fi although the radio supports WPA3
rule.wifi.wps.explanation: The WPS PIN method can be guessed in hours on many devices and then reveals the passphrase; the push button lets anyone with brief physical access join. Most networks never use WPS after setup. A warning for the PIN method, info for the push button (and NFC or an unknown method).
rule.wifi.wps.title: Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) is turned on

rule.security.default-password.title: Device uses its factory password
rule.security.default-password.explanati: Factory passwords are the first thing anyone in the network tries; on small switches they give full control (VLANs included). Reported when the login Signalbox was given is the vendor's documented default (NETGEAR Plus `password`, TP-Link Easy Smart and Omada `admin`/`admin`, MikroTik `admin` without a password, OpenWrt `root` without a password), compared in memory without trying anything, or when the device itself says it still has its default password (FRITZ!Box). OpenWrt can also be probed for an empty root password (`probe_empty_root_password`, off by default).
rule.account.signalbox-privileged.title: Signalbox reads with more privileges than it needs
rule.account.signalbox-privileged.explan: Signalbox only needs to read, and each integration's setup guide describes a read-only login (docs/adapters/, "read-only user"). Reported when the login it was given may do more than that guide's login, typically the administrator account. A device that may receive changes from Signalbox needs a login that may write; that is taken into account. Devices whose integration has no smaller login (FRITZ!Box, small switches) are not reported.
rule.account.admin-default-name.title: Administrator account with the default name
rule.account.admin-default-name.explanat: An enabled administrator account named `admin` that logs in with a password, on a device whose management address is in a network with clients or Wi-Fi: anyone there only has to guess the password. Renaming it (or using another account and disabling it) takes that half away. Accounts that only log in with a key are left out.
rule.account.no-password.title: Account without a password
rule.account.no-password.explanation: An enabled account that has no password logs in with the name alone (unless the device only accepts a key for it). Reported where the device says whether a password is set (OpenWrt rpcd logins, the Omada device account).
rule.account.stale.title: Administrator account not used for a long time
rule.account.stale.explanation: An enabled administrator account that did not log in for 90 days, or never while Signalbox has known the device for 90 days, is a forgotten way in. Only for devices that report login times (MikroTik); Signalbox's own login is left out. Needs the observation history clock.

rule.wifi.regulatory.title: Wi-Fi channel or power not allowed in the radio's country
rule.wifi.regulatory.explanation: Each country allows only some channels and a maximum transmit power; the radio's country code selects them. A channel (or a part of a wide channel) that is not allowed there is either not used (the radio does not start) or makes the network invisible to clients set to the right country; 6 GHz is not available in every country; power above the limit is illegal and disturbs radar and others. The usual cause is a country code copied with a configuration. A channel list the device reports itself wins over Signalbox's small regulatory table, which is a guide and not legal advice. An error for a channel that is not allowed, a warning for power above the limit, information for a missing country code.

rule.wifi.channel-busy.title: Wi-Fi channel busy
rule.wifi.channel-busy.explanation: The radio reported that its channel was busy most of the time at the last read: its own clients, neighbouring networks and other radio sources share the air time, so every client waits longer to send. From 60 % this is reported for information, from 80 % as a warning. One read is a snapshot: a short peak (a large download) can trigger it, a channel that is busy at every read needs action. Radios that do not report their utilisation are skipped.
rule.wifi.radar-hit.title: Radar detected on a Wi-Fi channel
rule.wifi.radar-hit.explanation: On the 5 GHz radar (DFS) channels an access point must leave the channel when it detects radar, and may not come back for half an hour; its clients lose the network for a moment and the radio moves to another channel. Reported when the radio says radar was detected within the last 24 hours, or that it left its channel because of radar. Real radar near airports and weather stations, but also false detections by some hardware, cause this: if it repeats, a channel outside 52-144 avoids it.
rule.wifi.legacy-standard.title: Radio set to an old Wi-Fi standard
rule.wifi.legacy-standard.explanation: The radio supports a newer Wi-Fi standard than the one it is set to, so every client, also a new one, is limited to the old standard's speed and efficiency. Newer standards stay compatible with older clients, so the newest mode the radio supports (up to Wi-Fi 6, 802.11ax) is usually the right choice. A warning for 802.11a, b and g (no MIMO, no wider channels), information otherwise. Radios that do not report what they support are skipped.

rule.lag.mode-mismatch.title: The two ends of a link aggregation use different modes
rule.lag.mode-mismatch.explanation: Both ends of a LAG must agree on how it works: LACP on both (at least one of them active), or static on both. LACP on one end and a static LAG on the other forms no aggregation on the LACP side and sends frames over every cable on the static side: loops, duplicated frames or silent loss follow. Two passive LACP ends never start. A Linux bond in active-backup, balance-tlb or balance-alb mode works towards single switch ports, not towards a LAG. Checked where both devices report the mode and every known cable of the LAG ends in one LAG of one other device.
rule.lag.member-not-selected.title: A LAG member is up but does not carry traffic
rule.lag.member-not-selected.explanation: LACP aggregates a member only when the far end answers on that cable with the same system and key as on the other members. A member that is up but not collecting and distributing usually goes to the wrong device or port, or its far end is not in the LAG, or it runs at another speed or duplex. The LAG works without it, with less bandwidth and no redundancy for that cable. Checked where the device reports the LACP state of its members.
rule.lag.partner-mismatch.title: The members of a LAG lead to different LACP partners
rule.lag.partner-mismatch.explanation: Every member of one LAG must reach the same LACP partner: the same system (its system MAC address) and the same key. Members with different partners are cabled to two devices, or to ports of two LAGs on the far end; LACP then uses only the members of one partner. Switch stacks and MLAG pairs present one system id and do not trigger this. Checked where the device reports the partner of its members.

rule.stp.several-roots.title: More than one spanning tree root in one network
rule.stp.several-roots.explanation: Switches and bridges that are connected by cables should form one spanning tree with one root bridge. When the bridges of one network name different root bridges, the spanning tree messages (BPDUs) do not get from one part to the other: a switch or bridge between them has spanning tree off and drops them, or a port filters them. A loop through both parts is then not blocked by anyone. Only bridges that report their root are compared.
rule.stp.root-not-core.title: Spanning tree root is not the core of the network
rule.stp.root-not-core.explanation: The root bridge of a spanning tree should be the central device (the router's switch or the core switch): all traffic flows towards the root, and the links that are blocked follow from where it is. The root is the bridge with the lowest priority, and on a tie the lowest MAC address, so a cheap switch with the factory priority 32768 often wins by chance. Reported when the root is another device although a gateway or the most connected switch of the network takes part in the spanning tree.
rule.stp.disabled-with-redundancy.title: Spanning tree off on a bridge in a loop
rule.stp.disabled-with-redundancy.explan: A bridge or switch without spanning tree forwards everything, so two paths between the same switches (two cables without a link aggregation, or a ring over several switches) form a loop: broadcasts circle forever and the network stops within seconds. Reported when the known cables of a bridge with spanning tree off lead to the same device twice, or to switches that are connected to each other another way, and no device on that loop blocks a port. Loop detection of simple switches counts as protection.
rule.stp.topology-changes.title: Frequent spanning tree topology changes
rule.stp.topology-changes.explanation: Every topology change makes the switches of the network forget their MAC address tables and flood traffic until they have learnt them again; frequent changes come from a port that goes up and down (a bad cable, a client that sleeps, a port that is not an edge port). Reported from 20 changes when they average more than 6 per hour since the device started.
rule.stp.client-port-not-edge.title: Port to a client is not an edge port
rule.stp.client-port-not-edge.explanatio: A port that only has a client behind it (a PC, a printer, an access point without its own bridge in the tree) should be an edge port (PortFast): it then forwards as soon as the link comes up, and its link changes do not count as topology changes. A port that is not an edge port waits up to 30 seconds after every link change (classic STP) and makes the switches flush their address tables. Reported for ports of a bridge with spanning tree that say they are not edge ports, have clients and no known switch behind them.

rule.wifi.rogue-ssid.title: Foreign access point with one of your Wi-Fi names
rule.wifi.rogue-ssid.explanation: An access point that is not one of yours broadcasts one of your Wi-Fi names (SSIDs). Phones and laptops join any network with a remembered name, so this can be an evil twin that tries to catch your devices and their traffic, or simply a forgotten old router, a repeater or a neighbour who picked the same name. Based on the access points your radios heard: a controller's rogue AP list, or a scan you turned on. An access point is yours when its BSSID belongs to one of your WLANs or ports; scan results are only compared where every access point with that name reports its BSSID. The finding does not show the foreign BSSID: the device's neighbours list does.
rule.wifi.channel-crowded.title: Wi-Fi channel shared with many neighbours
rule.wifi.channel-crowded.explanation: The radio heard at least 3 foreign access points stronger than -80 dBm on a channel overlapping its own. They all share the air time, so your clients wait longer to send, more so when the channel is also busy (wifi.channel-busy). Where the radio heard a channel with fewer neighbours, the finding names it. Based on a scan (off by default) or a controller's rogue AP list; radios without one are skipped.
